idiom_name: conditional and mapped types as type-level traits (with infer)
implementation_notes: TypeScript keeps the descriptor idea at the type level: a generic conditional type (T extends X ? A : B), infer and mapped types with key remapping compute per-type results from a type's properties and carry the associated payload (Flatten<T> extracts the element type, MessageOf<T> yields T['message'] or never) - what a traits class does at value level - and all of it is erased at build time. Direct constraints (T extends { message: unknown }) state a requirement where a descriptor would only document it, and at runtime the JavaScript protocols (well-known symbols, duck-typed methods) still decide behaviour: a TypeScript trait never produces a dispatch table, so values crossing the boundary must be validated there.
pitfalls: Conditional types are distributive over naked type parameters: T extends X ? A : B applied to a union is applied per member (wrap both sides in tuples to disable distributivity), which turns one intended decision into a union of decisions.
Only the true branch narrows the type parameter; the false branch is still typed with the original T, so 'otherwise' branches can compile with a type the runtime value never has.

Nothing is checked at runtime: trait types are erased, a value typed any satisfies every constraint (so an untyped boundary bypasses the check), and structural typing accepts any object that happens to have the right members.
